**In Praise of Lichen**

There is a rock behind a farmhouse in the north of Scotland that I have never seen, but which I think about more than I think about most places I have actually been. It is a fairly ordinary lump of granite, and it is covered in a crust of pale green-grey lichen, and a geologist who measured the patches decided that some of them had been growing since roughly the time the Romans left Britain. Not the rock, which is of course far older. The lichen. The living thing. A smear of something no thicker than a coat of paint, quietly persisting for sixteen centuries while empires assembled and dissolved a few hundred miles to the south.

I find that I return to lichen whenever I want to remember that the world is stranger than the categories I've been handed for it.

Take the most basic question: what is it? For most of the history of biology, the answer was "a plant, probably a moss of some kind." Then in 1867 a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener proposed something that struck his colleagues as slightly obscene. A lichen, he said, was not one organism but two: a fungus, which provided the structure and clung to the surface, and an alga, which lived inside it and did the photosynthesis. The fungus was, in his rather Victorian framing, a master enslaving a captive. The scientific establishment was appalled. It offended the idea that a species was a thing with clean edges. It offended the idea that nature, at bottom, was competitive. Schwendener was more or less right, though we've softened the language since. The current word is symbiosis, and the current understanding is that the arrangement is even messier than he imagined: many lichens include a third partner, a yeast, discovered only in 2016, hiding in the outer layer and apparently having been there all along, in plain sight, unnoticed for a hundred and fifty years of intensive study.

So a lichen is a committee. It has no single genome. If you sequence one, you get several organisms' worth of DNA tangled together, and the "species" you name is really the name of a relationship. That should be more unsettling than it is. We are quite used to thinking of ourselves as individuals, single things with single boundaries, and here is a common piece of the landscape — you have walked past ten thousand of them — that simply refuses to be an individual in that sense. It is a *we* pretending to be an *it*.

And it is astonishingly good at being alive. Lichens grow on bare rock in Antarctica, where nothing else does. They grow in deserts, on the sides of buildings in polluted cities, on the backs of beetles, on gravestones, on the glass of old windows. In 2005 the European Space Agency attached samples of two lichen species to the outside of a capsule and exposed them to open space for about fifteen days: vacuum, hard ultraviolet, cosmic radiation, temperature swings of a hundred and fifty degrees. Then they brought them back and watered them. The lichens resumed photosynthesizing as if they'd been through a slightly inconvenient winter. They are, as far as anyone can tell, among the toughest complex living things on the planet, and they achieve this by being almost unbelievably undramatic. They do not run, fight, or flee. They shut down when conditions are bad and wait. Sometimes they wait for years.

The waiting is what I love most. Some crustose lichens grow at a rate of a fraction of a millimeter a year. You could stare at one for your whole life and never see it move, and yet it is moving, the way a glacier is moving, on a schedule that makes our own lives look like a match being struck. There's a discipline called lichenometry that uses this: because certain species grow at known, glacially steady rates, you can measure the diameter of a patch and estimate when the rock beneath it was last disturbed. Lichens have been used to date moraines, rockfalls, the retreat of ice sheets, the earthquake that toppled a wall. They are clocks that nobody wound, ticking on every mountainside, waiting for someone to bother to read them.

I think what lichens correct in me is a certain assumption about what counts as success. We tend to admire the fast and the large: the tree that shoots up, the predator, the thing with a heartbeat you can hear. Lichens have none of that. They have no roots, no leaves, no flowers, no way to move toward what they need. They simply arrive, in the form of a few cells carried by wind or rain, and if the surface is bare enough that nothing else wants it, they stay. They make the surface habitable, slowly breaking down the rock, catching dust, building the first thin film of what will eventually become soil. Then mosses arrive and outcompete them, then grasses, then shrubs, then trees, and the lichen has by that point moved on to the next bare rock, having made itself unnecessary. Almost every forest on Earth stands on ground that lichens prepared first and were then evicted from. It is a strange kind of triumph: to be the reason something exists and to be entirely forgotten by it.

I don't want to make lichen into a moral lesson. That is a lazy thing to do to a living creature — to use it as a mirror. But I'll admit the shape of its existence is consoling. It suggests that there is more than one way to be here. That partnership can be so total it becomes a new kind of thing. That you can be tiny and slow and still outlast the Romans. That a life can consist almost entirely of enduring, and that enduring, done long enough, becomes a kind of building.

Next time you pass a wall or a gravestone or an old fence post, look closely. The orange and grey and pale green patches are not stains. They are ancient, collaborative, patient, and alive, and they were there before you and will be there after. It's oddly cheering, I find. The world is being quietly held together by things that are in no hurry at all.
